items.q: What is the difference between an executive order and a law?
items.a: A law is a statute enacted by Congress. An executive order is a written directive in which the President sets policy, and such orders tend to be directed to government officials. To have legal effect, an order must rest on the President's powers under the Constitution or on power Congress has delegated, and it cannot override a statute.

sources.label: Congressional Research Service, Executive Orders: An Introduction

items.a: An agency official or other executive officer usually writes the first draft, which can start with a request from the President or with a proposal from an agency. Under the standing procedure, the draft goes to the Office of Management and Budget, which shares it with interested agencies for comment. It then goes to the Attorney General, whose Office of Legal Counsel reviews it for form and legality, and then to the President, who decides whether to sign. Not every order follows this process.

sources.label: Congressional Research Service, Executive Orders: An Introduction

items.q: Who can overturn an executive order?
items.a: A President can amend or revoke an executive order, and a later President can generally revoke or modify any earlier order. Congress can nullify the legal effect of an order that was issued under power Congress delegated to the President. Courts can also review an order and hold it unconstitutional when the President had no authority for it, either from the Constitution or from Congress.

sources.label: Congressional Research Service, Executive Orders: An Introduction

items.q: Who has to follow an executive order?
items.a: Executive orders tend to be directed toward government officials, so the officials and agencies of the executive branch are the ones an order directs. Some orders are effective only against federal agencies or people acting as their officers, agents, or employees. Agency action that implements an order can also affect outside parties, who can challenge that action in court.

sources.label: Congressional Research Service, Executive Orders: An Introduction

items.q: Who signed the most executive orders?
items.a: Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the most executive orders, with a total of 3,726 over 12.12 years in office. The table counts executive orders only, not memoranda or other written presidential directives.
